reading_plan: Source title: Multi-criteria thermoeconomic and thermodynamic assessments of the desalination-integrated two-phase liquid-immersion data center cooling system. Source type: peer_reviewed_paper. This is a densely written, two-column engineering research article, with a summary, numbered sections, extensive displayed equations, three tables, ten figures, nomenclature, references, and three coefficient appendices. I will follow its printed order, normally taking about 200-350 words per step and using shorter natural units for tightly linked equations, tables, and closing material. The initial overview concerns this texture only. I distinguish the authors' prose from my readings of displayed elements; all claims and supports below are paraphrased. Locations give printed pages and PDF page numbers. Citation numerals retain their printed content (superscripting is flattened), and reference entries retain the source's wording with line-wrap hyphenation joined.

reading_path.location: p. 10453 (PDF p. 1), Summary
reading_path.moves: Proposes a design, states its purpose and scope, and previews numerical findings and a feasibility inference. This is the authors' opening synopsis; its reported results have not yet been developed in the reading.

claims.text: The authors propose using waste heat from two-phase liquid-immersion data center cooling to heat the feed of a direct contact membrane distillation module, aiming to reduce the economic drawback of cooling waste heat.
They select a cooling-load range of 0.7-1.5 kW and a membrane-area range of 5-75 cm², calling immersion cooling promising for heat-flux removal but under-researched for waste-heat management.
The summary reports maximum thermal and exergy efficiencies of 64.5% and 53.7%, and a maximum distilled-water production of 6.13 kg/day at the largest cooling load and membrane area.
The hybrid has higher capital and operating costs than stand-alone cooling, but the authors take its reported 3.72-year payback as evidence of economic feasibility.
The summary gives a levelized product cost of 2.69-5.33 SGD/h and a multiobjective trade-off at 1.1 kW with membrane area between 5.12 and 5.19 cm².

reading_path.meaning: The opening frames waste heat as both a cost problem and a usable resource, and promises several assessment methods. These are announced findings, not evidence already encountered; subsequent repetitions will be marked as returns to this synopsis.

claims.text: Liquids remove higher heat flux than air, making liquid cooling increasingly attractive for rapidly developing ICT facilities.

Indirect liquid cooling is more established but entails leakage risk in circulation piping and load-specific layout sizing; direct cooling avoids server/rack piping through dielectric-fluid contact and can be modified flexibly for different loads.

Jet impingement, spray cooling, and two-phase immersion are direct methods that can operate independently or with air cooling; latent heat transfer gives two-phase immersion more uniform equipment-surface temperatures.

claims.text: The authors claim that neither this hybrid design nor the use of two-phase immersion cooling waste heat for desalination has previously been investigated.
They present direct contact membrane distillation as a new clean-water-producing alternative, especially at low cooling loads.
They claim a new, system-specific exergy-cost matrix, alongside thermodynamic and economic assessments, can assist future immersion-cooling waste-heat studies.
They set optimization objectives of minimizing distilled-water and system-product costs and maximizing exergy efficiency, with cooling load constrained to 0.7-1.5 kW and membrane area to 5-75 cm².

reading_path.meaning: This is a formal restatement of the proposed contribution rather than its demonstration. The low-load gap now becomes explicit numerical scope, and the analysis methods are positioned as contributions in their own right.
